https://github.com/roc-lang/roc/issues/11594

@Richard Feldman, could you summarize some of the downsides and the "can of worms"? I don't have any clue, since it works so great in Zig. Maybe because Zig's type system is simpler?

The lack of this seriously limits the expressivity for some ideas, or require very complex workarounds. If I understood the downsides, maybe we could figure out some solution that doesn't have those downsides, yet enable all the use cases. Not necessarily a 1:1 port of the Zig builtin, just something that enables more concise and readable code.

sure! so here are some of the downsides I've seen in "expose a representation of the type as a value" in other languages:

  • if I can ask "get the representation of this type" of any type, and then programmatically get values from it (e.g. I can say "I see that this is a record with a field named foo whose type is Str, and also I can use that type info to access the value of that foo field at runtime), that means that module boundaries are no longer strictly enforced like they are today, because there's a workaround you can use to read the "private" data from any value anywhere.
    • That in turn means any package that does effectful functions involving network requests can now be used to exfiltrate any secret in the program, whereas today they need to be passed those secrets explicitly.
    • This is not a downside in Zig because Zig doesn't have opaque data types by design
    • This could be mitigated by having a rule like "you can only get the type info of a type whose internals you can access from here," but then that has to be reflected in the type system somehow; otherwise the compiler couldn't infer a type for the lambda |a| typeinfo a without introducing a new type for "a type variable whose typeinfo can be accessed from this scope"
  • Parametricity guarantees disappear; as the most basic example, today, a -> a has only one implementation. if you can get the type info of a as a value, you can make that function return a different value depending on what you pass in.
    • That in turn means you can no longer learn as much from type signatures anymore, e.g. List(a) -> List(a) would not longer tell you as much as it does today.
    • Again, Zig's comptime already doesn't guarantee parametricity, so this is not a downside for Zig.
  • Some compile-time warnings become either impossible or easily defeated, e.g. "this nominal record field is unused" is no longer something we can confidently say if anything asks for that type's info, because they could be doing something with the type info of that field, such that deleting the field would break the program.
    • Again, Zig already doesn't have a lot of "unused" warnings that Roc does, which I believe is mostly because of comptime reflection.
these are just the first ones that come to mind; there are others, but this is an example of the can of worms I am reluctant to open :sweat_smile:

It has the additional benefit of explicitly enabling/disabling reflection for a type.

The downside is that it's not available for structural types, which cover a significant chunk of use cases.

what use cases would this enable that we can't do today?

A few:

  • For a pure-Roc object persistence framework, it would allow nicer, readable schema/migration syntax and boilerplate-free code.
  • A SurrealDB client, similar to Niclas' roc-pg. However, SurrealDB has a much more powerful data model, e.g. it supports type unions in the database (but it's not tagged, so it can not use the the official encoder API), and returns nested data in CBOR, compared to the row+column output of Postgres.
  • Schema validation libraries (like Valibot/Zod), with more ergonomic syntax and comptime guarantees.
  • The ones I wrote in the issue.
  • Powerful comptime-checked templates.

There are much more, but since it's not currently possible, I instantly discard any idea that could be done with it.

Some of these use cases that are currently possible in a limited way, but this would make them much-much easier and powerful. Reflection in itself is not that much of a tool (except for API endpoint type generation for Elm/TypeScript), but pairing it with field access and maybe with an upgraded struct builder would unlock most of the use cases.
One example is to allow defining persisted objects as arbitrary structs, and automatically enabling constraints for every field that has a ForeignKey type.

A hacky workaround is possible by creating a fake parser, and parsing a fake item. But it's much more complex and fragile, and if we try to shoehorn solutions to APIs that weren't designed for this, it'll be buggy and quickly hit limitations.
On the other hand, if a sufficiently powerful reflection API is added, it could replace the encoder/parser APIs, since those could be implemented in userspace.
And maybe the struct builder too.

When I need some solution like this, I always evaluate some hacky workarounds based on the encoder and the struct builder API, but they are mostly complex and fragile, and usually I hit a limitation. I think that users are going to build hacks around these APIs, which (in my opinion) will be harmful to the Roc ecosystem in the long term.
And importantly: these hacks usually require much more time. That time could be spent on building actually useful things, not on working around artificial limitations.

Some more brainstorming, just a dump of probably bad ideas (but possibly some inspiration to someone). Some are use cases, some are possible solutions:

  • I would like a struct builder where the name of the field is available to the function. However, this would only solve some of the limitations, and it would add another limited API.
  • Reverse-record-builder, where an already existing record is iterated field by field. Another limited API, only for some use cases. It's useful only when the field name can be decisive, but not when the field type is needed instead of the value.
  • It would be nice, if two structs could be zipped together, with the name also available. E.g. take a field from a struct, take the same-name field from another struct, and call a function with the name, the two values, and a combine function.

Here's an example that's not possible currently in a clean way.

This is a coarse concept for an object persistence library:

Post := {
    title: Str,
    content: Str,
}

User := {
    username: Str,
    # Incorrect, should be List(RecordId(Post))
    posts: List(Post),
}

Database := PersistenceEngine({
    users: User,
    posts: Post,
})

If a type has a table, it MUST be linked from other records via RecordId(type), and it's not possible to store the data inline. (Any other supported type is inlined.) Comptime checking would instruct the user to change it to a RecordId(Post) in the above example.

This kind of feature would make an (all-in-Roc) ECS much easier to implement. Today, the platform (or something associated with it) would need to take a list of types that are considered 'components' and generate a new 'world' type composed of them. I had also been considering ways of trying to abuse the encoder machinery for this, but I think it might end up not being sufficient, and if it did work it would boil down to a hacky version of this API. Essentially we run into the same problems as the database client, I think (component = column, world = table).

Having reflection also unlocks more ability for platforms to interact with existing native ECS libraries like flecs or bevy. To use these, the platform fundamentally needs some way to get type-level information to the native library without recompiling the platform.

The ability to do something like
Ok(val) = some_validation(SomeType.reflect_info())
is both very powerful and potentially a bit spooky. Like, if it's not dependent types it's certainly getting closer.

Another use case is writing type-safe migrations for databases. E.g. AddField({name: "posts", type: List(RecordId(User)) }), then the migration checker woud check if applying all the migration history would match the current schema.

Again, could be solved with a fake encoder. Partially. Then possibly find some cases where it's not possible to comptime check via the encoder API, because it's not flexible enough, then resorting to runtime crashes.

Richard Feldman said:

Dan G Knutson (and anyone else who has use cases in this area that aren't currently implementable) I'm curious to hear your thoughts!

struct-of-array (SoA) from a record is a likely contender use case.

Something along the lines of

Particle := {
    x : F32,
    y : F32,
    vx : F32,
    vy : F32,
}

ParticleSoA := SoA(Particle)

particles : ParticleSoA
particles = SoA.append(particles, {
    x: 1.0,
    y: 2.0,
    vx: 0.5,
    vy: 0.3,
})

Reflection could convert an arbitrary record into a Dict or List of field/value.

This would help the HTML DSL use case. For example in Joy :
https://github.com/niclas-ahden/joy-todomvc/blob/main/app.roc#L156

header(
        [class("header")],
        [
            h1([], [text("todos")]),
            input([
                class("new-todo"),
                placeholder("What needs to be done?"),
                value(model.draft),
                on_input(|s| UserTypedDraft(s)),
            ]),
        ],
    )

could become

header(
        { class: "header" },
        [
            h1({}, [text("todos")]),
            input({
                class: "new-todo",
                placeholder: "What needs to be done?",
                value: model.draft,
                on_input: |s| UserTypedDraft(s),
            }),
        ],
    )

which is closer to HTML and would avoid a bunch of user imports (class(), placeholder(), value(), on_input() which are here to normalize the attribute types) while remaining type checked.
I think, reflection could make HTML templating even simpler. A comptime-parsed string with a custom templating syntax. It could acces the corresponding struct fields and comptime check them.
